topic: Instantaneous Rate of Change and the Derivative

outline.topic: Instantaneous Rate of Change and the Derivative

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Average Speed Concept
sections.content: Recall that average speed is total distance divided by total time. Visually, this is the slope of a secant line connecting two distinct points (P and Q) on a position-time graph.
sections.example: A cheetah runs 100 meters in 5 seconds. Average speed = 20 m/s. Visually: A straight line connecting the start and end point on the distance curve.

sections.title: The Problem of 'Instantaneous' Speed
sections.content: What if we want to know the cheetah's speed at exactly 2 seconds? Our standard formula fails because the time interval becomes zero (division by zero). Introduce the idea of shrinking the interval.
sections.example: The cheetah's speedometer shows its exact speed at 2.00s. We move point Q closer and closer to point P on the graph.

sections.title: The Limit Process: Approaching the Tangent
sections.content: Explain that as the time interval Δt approaches zero, the secant line morphs into a tangent line. The slope of this tangent line represents the instantaneous rate of change.
sections.example: Animation: Point Q 'slides' along the curve toward P. The secant line tilts until it matches the curve's slope at exactly point P.

sections.title: Defining the Derivative
sections.content: Formally define the derivative as the limit of the difference quotient: f'(x) = lim(h→0) [f(x+h) - f(x)] / h. This is the mathematical 'tool' to calculate the instantaneous rate of change.
sections.example: Applying the formula to a simple function like f(x) = x² to find the general slope at any point x.

sections.title: Application: Real-world Significance
sections.content: Summarize that the derivative is not just a math symbol; it is the 'local' behavior of a function. Used in physics (velocity), economics (marginal cost), and biology (growth rates).
sections.example: A rocket launch: The derivative tells us the exact vertical velocity at any second t, crucial for ensuring the rocket doesn't break under pressure.
